newsitem.title: USA: Abundant U.S. crops, low food price rise in '97.
newsitem.headline: Abundant U.S. crops, low food price rise in '97.

text.p: U.S. Farmers will open the throttle on output in 1997, the first year of the "Freedom to Farm" law, producing abundant U.S. crops and starting a period of minimal increases in food prices, the Agriculture Department said on Monday.
Food prices will rise more slowly than the overall inflation rate in coming years and should average 2.4 percent a year, the department said at its annual Outlook Forum.

Department Economist Annette Clauson said this year's food inflation would likely be lower than the 3.3 percent of 1996 -- the first year this decade it exceeded the overall inflation rate and also the first it topped three percent.

Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman has repeatedly warned the European Union against unfair subsidies on farm exports. But a top-ranking EU administrator, D.F. Roberts, said in prepared remarks that Europe had "neither the budgetary resources nor the intention" of provoking an export war with the United States.
Although the United States has refrained from retaliating against EU grain subsidies so far, big crops have raised the specter of another price war later this year.

Exports provide nearly 25 cents out of every dollar in U.S. farm receipts. The export market is commonly regarded as the road to prosperity for U.S. agriculture because of rapidly growing food demand around the world.

U.S. agriculture exports would total $55.5 billion this fiscal year, down from the record $59.8 billion of last year, the department said in its first forecast of the year. Most of the drop-off would be due to lower grain and oilseed prices.

The new "Freedom to Farm" law removes most federal controls on farming, letting farmers shift from crop to crop as they wish. Strong crop production was forecast as a result as farmers can aggressively pursue profits.
For this year, it would mean more corn, wheat and soybeans than last year but less cotton and rice. Export tonnage would be strong and thin U.S. stockpiles would swell modestly.

There was some scepticism about an upturn in the wheat harvest. Winter wheat seedings, at 48 million acres, were the lowest since 1978. Large spring wheat sowings would be needed to reach the department's forecast of 72 million acres of wheat.
Corn output was pegged at 9.63 billion bushels, wheat at 2.35 billion bushels, soybeans at 2.42 billion bushels, cotton at 17.3 million bales and rice at 166.1 million hundredweight.

By comparison, output last year was 9.29 billion bushels of corn, 2.28 billion bushels of wheat, 2.38 billion bushels of soybeans, 18.95 million bales of cotton and 171.3 million hundredweight of rice.

Beef production, mimicking a drop in cattle numbers, was forecast to fall by 0.8 percent this year, to 25.4 billion pounds. Pork would rise two percent to 17.5 billion pounds and broiler chicken output would be 27.8 billion pounds, up 5.8 percent.

Keith Collins, the department's chief economist, has said the downturn in the cattle cycle provided the basis for concern about future food inflation. A weather "shock" to crops could drive up grain prices and cut meat output, engendering higher grocery prices, he said.
